posts.linkedin:
If all you want is a sharper rate, call your bank.

Banks are competitive on price. If your rate is the only thing bothering you, one phone call to your lender's retention team will usually fix it. You don't need us for that.

Where we earn our keep is structure: how the debt is split, what's secured against what, where the offsets sit, and whether the setup still makes sense for the next thing you want to do. Those decisions compound for years. A rate discount is a footnote.

So before you refinance, ask one question: is this a rate problem or a structure problem?

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.myth: Pay the investment loan down first. Debt is debt.
cards.reality: Most of our clients put repayments on the home loan instead.
cards.because: Interest on an investment loan is usually tax-deductible; interest on your own home isn’t. Worth a conversation with your accountant.

posts.linkedin:
"Debt is debt. Pay it all down."

We hear this a lot from investors, and it's the one place we'll gently push back.

Not all debt costs you the same. Interest on an investment loan is usually tax-deductible. Interest on the home you live in isn't. So every dollar you put against the home loan saves you after-tax money, while every dollar against the investment loan reduces a deduction.

Our general view: keep investment debt interest-only, point your repayments and your offset at the home loan, and revisit if you ever plan to move into the investment.

It's a conversation to have with your accountant alongside your broker, because the tax side depends on your situation.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.linkedin:
A rough rule of thumb we give first-home buyers: your borrowing capacity is about five times your income.

That's before HECS, car loans and credit cards come off it, and before any lender has run your actual payslips. It's not a quote. It's a starting budget so your weekend searching isn't wasted on the wrong price bracket.

The real number moves a lot between lenders. The same payslips can come back with meaningfully different answers, which is why we run several before telling anyone what they can spend.

General information only, not personal advice.

Buying your first home? The loan is the easy bit.

Getting finance approved is the part everyone worries about and, with the right preparation, the part that goes fastest. The hard part is everything around it: working out if a place is actually good value, spotting a body corporate problem before it's yours, knowing what to offer and when to walk, and keeping the contract and settlement on track.

That's where we spend most of our time with first-home buyers. You do the inspecting, because how a place feels when you walk in matters most. We do the data, the due diligence and the negotiation alongside you, all the way to the keys.

cards.hook: The bank’s maximum is not your number.
cards.so_what: Ask for the comfortable figure and the stretch figure, then plan on the first.

posts.linkedin:
The bank's maximum is not your number.

When we quote borrowing capacity we give the comfortable figure first. Could we squeeze more if we pushed? Usually. But approval and affordability are different things, and living at the very edge of what a lender will give you rarely buys a better life.

So we show two numbers: the one you'd be comfortable repaying through a couple of rate moves, and the stretch. Then we plan around the first and keep the second in the drawer for when something genuinely special comes up.

General information only, not personal advice.

A question to ask yourself this week: if your repayments rose $200 a month, which part of your budget would feel it first?

Not a trick question. On a typical loan a 0.25 percentage point move is roughly that, and the RBA meets on Tuesday. Knowing the answer before it happens is the difference between a plan and a scramble.

Stress-testing your own numbers once a year is the cheapest insurance there is.
